query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Trace doping of low concentrations (∼0.2 at.%) of cerium into a conventional AlCoCrFeNi–based high-entropy bond coat will promote the in‐situ formation of a Ce‐enriched gradient interlayer at the bond coat/TBC interface, thereby improving the adhesion of the thermally grown oxide scale and reducing its spallation under cyclic ultra‐high temperature conditions and CMAS exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) bond coat prepared by laser cladding with a mixed FCC/BCC microstructure, as used in existing thermal barrier coating systems, without any reactive element doping.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace amount (~0.2 at.%) of cerium during alloy preparation so that Ce is homogeneously dissolved and subsequently segregates to form a gradient interlayer during service exposure.
generation.conditions: Cyclic high-temperature conditions at approximately 900 °C in corrosive atmospheres that simulate molten salt/CMAS exposure, replicating service-like environments for TBC systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A Ce-enriched interfacial layer (or nano-clusters of CeOx) forms at the bond coat/TGO and substrate interface, creating a graded microstructure that acts as a diffusion barrier and enhances oxide adherence.
generation.mechanism: Cerium, as a reactive rare-earth element, is known to segregate to grain boundaries and interfaces. Its presence promotes the formation of a stable, dense, and adherent α-Al2O3 scale by impeding rapid cation diffusion and suppressing the growth of discontinuous oxide phases. This minimizes stress buildup and spallation during thermal cycling. Additionally, the graded Ce distribution reduces the impact of CMAS infiltration by hindering its diffusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an untreated bond coat, the Ce-doped coating is expected to show a reduction in the spallation area (by an estimated 20–30% under similar hot corrosion tests), a thinner and more uniform thermally grown oxide scale, and improved long-term durability and interfacial bonding reliability during cyclic thermal and CMAS corrosive exposures.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the undoped AlCoCrFeNi-based EHEA bond coat as previously characterized (e.g., spallation areas and oxide adhesion measured under 900 °C cyclic corrosion conditions).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects should persist under typical TBC operating conditions (around 900 °C with molten salt/CMAS exposure). However, the intervention might be less effective if the Ce concentration surpasses a critical threshold that could perturb the alloy’s phase stability or if the service temperature exceeds the range where Ce segregation and oxide stabilization are effective.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal extrapolates from evidence that trace reactive elements (e.g., Y and Hf) can form beneficial gradient layers (PMC10488378::web::015::4_conclusions, PMC10488483::web::010::3_results_and_discussion) and from findings that rare-earth elements in high-entropy strategies improve CMAS resistance (PMC11678358::web::004::1_introduction). While reactive element doping is well established in conventional superalloys, the direct effects of Ce in HEA bond coats remains uncertain, especially regarding its long-term segregation kinetics and phase compatibility in the HEA’s complex microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA bond coats using identical laser cladding parameters; one set with an added 0.2 at.% cerium and one set untreated. Subject both sets to cyclic thermal exposure at 900 °C for 60 hours in a controlled environment with a molten salt/CMAS mixture. Characterize the microstructure (using EBSD and TEM) and measure TGO adherence, spallation area, and oxide scale thickness post-testing.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of spallation area (percentage of total surface area spalled) using image analysis.
Thickness and uniformity of the thermally grown oxide layer via SEM cross-sectional analysis.
Adhesion strength between the oxide layer and bond coat via standardized pull-off tests.
Identification of Ce segregation and gradient formation at the interface via energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or atom probe tomography (APT).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ce-doped bond coat fails to show a statistically significant reduction (less than 10% difference) in spallation area, does not exhibit a Ce-enriched interfacial gradient, or if its TGO adhesion and overall durability under cyclic hot corrosion conditions are not measurably improved compared to the undoped baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
